title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance (Guidelines + ADRs)
author: Ava Martinez
body:
Summary:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and engineering standards across core areas: API design, coding/linting conventions, infrastructure configuration, model-serving best practices, observability requirements, performance targets, and the ADRs (architectural decision records) that capture trade-offs. It is intended as the canonical reference for new services, major changes, and cross-team reviews.

Audience:
- Service owners and tech leads
- Platform and SRE teams
- Model onboarding and applied ML engineers

Table of contents:
1) Principles and cross-cutting goals
2) API standards
3) Coding & repo standards
4) Infra and IaC standards
5) Model-serving standards
6) Observability standards
7) Performance SLOs and benchmarks
8) ADRs and change process
9) Appendix: examples and CLI snippets

1) Principles and cross-cutting goals
- Design for predictable production economics: latency, throughput, and unit cost are first-class design inputs.
- API stability for customers: backwards compatible defaults and formal deprecation windows.
- Platform-first: prefer building on Redwood Platform primitives (auth, routing, tracing) instead of bespoke implementations.
- Observable and debuggable: every service must expose metrics, structured logs, and traces.
- Automatable operations: all config required for day-2 ops must be codified (IaC, config-as-code).

2) API standards
Overview:
APIs at Redwood are public (external) or internal (service-to-service). Both follow the same design constraints but differ in auth and SLA. Use REST/gRPC consistently per team guidelines below.
Standards:
- Versioning: All public APIs must include a path version (e.g., /v1/). Minor contract changes require a new route or feature flag; breaking changes require a major version.
- Idempotency: write endpoints must be idempotent or accept an idempotency key.
- Error model: follow JSON-API style error objects with fields: code, message, request_id, retry_after (if rate-limited). Example:
  {
    "error": {"code": "INVALID_PROMPT", "message": "Prompt exceeds 64k tokens", "request_id": "abc-123"}
  }
- Pagination: use cursor-based pagination for large result sets; include next_cursor and has_more.
- Rate limiting: implement per-API and per-customer quotas; respond with 429 and Retry-After header.
- Telemetry hooks: every API handler must emit a request lifecycle metric and attach tracing context.
- Schema-first: APIs should be defined with OpenAPI 3.1 (REST) or protobufs (gRPC) and stored in the central API repo.
Compatibility & deprecation policy:
1. Announce deprecations 90 days in advance for internal-only changes, 180 days for public APIs.
2. Provide automatic fallback routing for 60 days after removing a route at the gateway level.

3) Coding & repo standards
Repository layout:
- One primary service per repo unless strongly coupled (exceptions require platform approval).
- Standard directories: /cmd, /internal, /pkg, /api, /deploy, /tests.
Tooling & CI:
- Mandatory linters: gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, black/isort/flake8 for Python, eslint/prettier for JS/TS.
- PR checks: unit tests, integration smoke tests (or test harness), static analysis, license check.
- Branch strategy: trunk-based development with short-lived feature branches; release tags are semver.
Code conventions highlights:
- API surface should be small and documented with examples.
- No business logic in handlers: handlers orchestrate calls to well-tested modules.
- Use typed errors and return structured error objects (see API error model).
- Secrets: never checked into source; use Secrets Manager references in IaC.
Security:
- All services must pass a dependency vulnerability scan before merge.
- Use SCA tooling (e.g., Dependabot or Renovate) configured to auto-open PRs for patch releases.

4) Infrastructure & IaC standards
Principles:
- All infra changes are code-reviewed and stored in terraform modules in the terraform monorepo.
- Environments: dev/test/staging/prod with automated promotion pipelines.
- Network: default deny security groups and least privilege for service accounts.
Standards:
- Moduleization: use standard modules for VPC, subnets, load balancers, autoscaling groups, and GPU pools.
- Secrets: KMS + secrets manager; rotation policy = 90 days for service keys, 365 days for long-lived certs.
- CI/CD: GitOps model; manifests and helm charts are stored with apps; deployment pipelines must include a canary stage.
- Capacity and scaling: define min/max for each autoscaling group and use metrics-based policies (CPU/GPU utilization, request queue length).
Example terraform snippet (helm release):
| resource | module | notes |
|---|---|---|
| aws_autoscaling_group | platform-gpu-pool | min=2, max=50, instance_type=p4d |

5) Model-serving standards
Goal:
Ensure model serving is reliable, cost-efficient, and compatible with Redwood runtime features (KV caching, batching, quantized kernels).
Onboarding checklist for new model variants:
1. Model card: include architecture, supported sequence lengths, tokenization, estimated vRAM, licensing.
2. Perf profile: latency and throughput curves across sequence lengths and batch sizes (CSV attached to onboarding PR).
3. Quantization profile: recommended quantization levels and accuracy impact.
4. Fallback mapping: compatible model variants for degraded capacity.
Serving constraints:
- Every model variant must declare: recommended_batch_size, max_seq_len, warmup_inference (boolean), kv_cache_compatible (boolean).
- Default runtime flags: continuous_batching=true, prefix_kv_cache_enabled=true.
- Healthchecks: liveness (ping model with a lightweight tokenized prompt) and readiness (load weights and validate KV cache warmup).
- Versioning: immutable model artifacts with content-hash version IDs; model aliases for routing (e.g., gptx-7b:latest).
Operational runbook highlights:
1. If latency SLO is violated for >5m, automatically route traffic to fallback variant and page oncall.
2. For OOM errors, capture coredump and offload model to analysis cluster; notify model owner.

6) Observability standards
Metrics:
- Use Prometheus format and the platform metrics registry. Standard metrics per service: request_latency_seconds (histogram), request_count_total (counter with labels route/status_code/model_variant), token_produced_total (counter), batch_size_distribution (histogram).
- SLO-derived metrics must be exported with the labels used by SLO dashboards (team, service, env).
Logging:
- Structured JSON logs with at minimum fields: timestamp, level, service, env, request_id, trace_id, user_id (if present), message.
- PII: redact fields marked as PII during ingestion; never log full prompt content for externally-facing requests unless approved and encrypted-at-rest.
Tracing:
- Use W3C Trace Context. Span naming convention: service.operation.resource. Include model_variant and routing_decision as span attributes for model-serving flows.
Dashboards & alerts:
- Standard dashboards: Overview (latency, errors, throughput), Model performance (per-variant latency/throughput), Cost dashboard (GPU hours, vRAM utilization).
- Alerting thresholds: High error rate (>1% 5m), Latency p95 > SLO * 1.5 for 5m, Queue depth > 75th percentile for 10m.

7) Performance SLOs and benchmarking
Company-wide SLOs:
- API request latency (interactive endpoints): p95 latency <= 200ms for small sequence lengths (<=256 tokens) on hosted tier.
- Model-serving token throughput: maintain required tokens/sec per GPU as published in the model catalog.
- Availability: 99.9% for hosted control plane routes, 99.5% for dedicated/private managed endpoints (SLAs may differ per contract).
Benchmarking process:
1. Define workload profile (seq length distribution, prompt mix, concurrency).
2. Run baseline perf suite on the target runtime/hardware.
3. Produce perf report: p50/p90/p95 latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, memory utilization.
4. Validate cost-per-token and include quantization impacts.
Example perf target table:
| model_variant | seq_len | target_p95_ms | tokens_sec_per_gpu | notes |
| gptx-7b-int8 | 256 | 180 | 1200 | recommended quantization int8 |
| gptx-13b-fp16 | 512 | 300 | 900 | use on dedicated pool |

8) ADRs and change process
How ADRs are authored and accepted:
- Create an ADR in the architecture repo as a markdown file named YYYYMMDD-title.md. Include motivation, alternatives considered, decision, and consequences.
- Review: At least two reviewers from infra/platform and the affected owner team.
- Acceptance: Merge ADR after approvals; reference ADR in PRs that implement the change.
Common recent ADRs (summaries):
- ADR-2026-02-18: "Default to continuous batching for model-serving" — decision: enable continuous batching by default, with per-route opt-out. Reason: 25-40% reduction in token cost for typical workloads.
- ADR-2026-01-10: "OpenAPI-first for public REST routes" — decision: Require OpenAPI 3.1 schemas for external REST APIs to enable automated SDK generation.
- ADR-2025-12-05: "Model artifact immutability and content-hash versioning" — decision: model artifacts are immutable and referenced by content-hash; simplifies rollbacks and caching.
Change management / rollouts:
1. Prepare a rollout plan in the PR describing canary %s, metrics to watch, and rollback criteria.
2. Use feature flags for staged rollout where applicable.
3. Post-rollout: update ADR (if relevant) and add notes to runbook.

9) Appendix: examples and CLI snippets
API schema example (OpenAPI fragment):
paths:
  /v1/generate:
    post:
      summary: Generate text
      requestBody:
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/GenerateRequest'

GenerateRequest schema snippet:
components:
  schemas:
    GenerateRequest:
      type: object
      properties:
        prompt:
          type: string
        max_tokens:
          type: integer
          default: 256

CLI example: deploy a canary to 10%
$ rdx deploy --service text-gen --env prod --canary 10 --image gcr.io/redwood/text-gen:v1.6.3

Debugging checklist for high latency:
1. Confirm traffic routing and model_variant (trace_id).
2. Check request metrics (p95, p99) for degradation start time.
3. Inspect GPU utilization and queue depth.
4. If queue depth high and p95 breached: scale out GPU pool or route to fallback variant.
5. Capture traces and attach to incident.

Ownership and support
- Primary owner: Architecture & Standards (eng)
- Secondary owners: Eng Platform, Eng SRE, Eng Serving Runtime, Applied ML
- Oncall: model-serving incidents escalate to eng-sre and runtime oncall per runbook.

Document maintenance
- This doc is reviewed quarterly. ADRs and standards will be updated as platform features (e.g., new batching kernels) land. Contributions are via PR in the architecture repo.

Feedback and questions: contact the Architecture & Standards owners or file an issue in the architecture repo.
